idiom_name: module augmentation / declaration merging for type-level growth + symbol or optional-member protocols at run time
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps JavaScript's runtime lookup - a symbol- or member-based probe narrowed by a user-defined type guard - and adds a compile-time way to grow a type you do not own: interfaces merge, so a consumer can reopen a library interface inside declare module 'the-module' { interface Request { user?: User } } and every importer sees the extra members without editing the library (the Express middleware pattern); the merge is additive, conflicts become compile errors, and it is the type-level half of 'extend without breaking clients'. The halves must stay in sync: augmentation changes types only, so the runtime capability must still exist - an optional member assigned by middleware, a symbol method, or a cast at the boundary - otherwise code type-checks and fails at run time. Because interfaces are open, the same mechanism can also make a library's contract stricter, which is how lib.es2015-style feature detection is modelled.
pitfalls: An augmentation silently does nothing unless the file is a module (it needs an import/export or export {}) and the specifier names the file where the type is declared (express vs express-serve-static-core) - both failure modes are no-ops, not errors.
Augmented members are type-only: the compiler is satisfied while the runtime value is missing, so the augmentation must be paired with the code that actually sets the member.
A type alias and a default export cannot be augmented, and an augmentation leaks into every compilation that includes the file.
Ambient declare module in a non-module file declares a new module instead of merging, shadowing the real typings.
